```{r setup}
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(classInt)
library(spdep)

crimes <- read.csv("../data/crimes.csv")
crimes_bng <- crimes |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(27700)
lsoa <- read.csv("../data/lsoa.csv") |> st_as_sf(wkt = "geometry", crs = 27700)
population <- read.csv("../data/population.csv")
wards <- read.csv("../data/wards.csv") |> st_as_sf(wkt = "geometry", crs = 27700)
city_centre <- wards |> filter(ward_name %in% c("Deansgate", "Piccadilly")) |> st_union()

lsoa_crime <- lsoa |>
  left_join(count(crimes, lsoa21cd, name = "crimes"), by = "lsoa21cd") |>
  left_join(population, by = "lsoa21cd") |>
  mutate(crimes = coalesce(crimes, 0L),
         rate_res = crimes / respop * 1000,
         rate_wkd = crimes / wkdpop * 1000)

theme_set(theme_void(base_size = 16))
purple <- "#5b2a86"
```

# Talk 1: Thinking spatially {background-color="#5b2a86"}

## Crime is concentrated in space

```{r concentration}
sorted <- sort(lsoa_crime$crimes, decreasing = TRUE)
k <- which(cumsum(sorted) >= sum(sorted) / 2)[1]
pct <- round(100 * k / length(sorted))
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
City centre to Fallowfield, June 2019: **`r pct`% of neighbourhoods (LSOAs) had half of all recorded crime**.

This pattern is so consistent across cities that Weisburd (2015) called it the **law of crime concentration**.

> "Everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things."
> Tobler (1970)
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r concentration-map, fig.width=6, fig.height=6}
ggplot(lsoa_crime) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = crimes >= sorted[k]), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey85", "#d7301f"),
                    labels = c("Other LSOAs", paste0("The ", k, " LSOAs with half of all crime")),
                    name = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
:::
::::

## Spatial data = attributes + location

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Vector** data model:

- **Points**: a crime, a pub
- **Lines**: a street, a bus route
- **Polygons**: a neighbourhood, a police beat

**Raster**: a grid of cells, e.g. a density surface or a satellite image

In R, `sf` stores vector data as a **table with a geometry column**.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r vector-types, fig.width=6, fig.height=6}
one_ward <- wards |> filter(ward_name == "Fallowfield")
pts <- st_filter(crimes_bng, one_ward)
bb <- st_bbox(one_ward)
line <- st_sfc(st_linestring(rbind(c(bb["xmin"], bb["ymin"] + 600), c(bb["xmax"], bb["ymax"] - 700))), crs = 27700) |>
  st_intersection(one_ward)
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = one_ward, fill = "#efe7f6", colour = purple, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_sf(data = line, colour = "grey30", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_sf(data = pts, colour = "#d7301f", size = 1.5) +
  labs(caption = "Polygon: Fallowfield ward. Points: its crimes. Line: an (illustrative) road.")
```
:::
::::

## Coordinate reference systems

The same crime, in two coordinate reference systems:

```{r crs-table}
p <- st_as_sf(crimes[1, ], coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326)
w <- round(st_coordinates(p), 5)
b <- round(st_coordinates(st_transform(p, 27700)))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  CRS = c("WGS 84 (EPSG:4326)", "British National Grid (EPSG:27700)"),
  x = c(paste(w[1], "degrees longitude"), paste(b[1], "metres east")),
  y = c(paste(w[2], "degrees latitude"), paste(b[2], "metres north"))
))
```

- **Geographic** (degrees on a sphere) vs **projected** (metres on a flat plane).
- Every flat map distorts something. Choose a projection to suit the area and the task.
- **Rules of thumb:** know each layer's CRS, match CRSs before combining layers, and measure in metres.

## The data are already a representation

- police.uk **snaps each crime to an anonymous map point**, e.g. "On or near Shopping Area".
- Crime data record only what is **reported and recorded**.
- Boundaries were drawn by someone, for some purpose (census, policing, elections).

**Representation → analytical decisions → interpretation**

➜ **Practical 0** (if new to R) and **Practical 1**

# Talk 2: Units of analysis and the stories maps tell {background-color="#5b2a86"}

## From incidents to places

- Aggregating points to areas changes the **unit of analysis** from crimes to neighbourhoods.
- Census areas (OA, LSOA, MSOA) are convenient: stable, with lots of attribute data. But they are not "neighbourhoods" as residents experience them.
- A map of **counts** mostly maps **where people and opportunities are**.

## Counts or rates? The denominator dilemma

```{r rates, fig.width=12, fig.height=4.8}
three <- bind_rows(
  lsoa_crime |> mutate(measure = "Count", value = crimes),
  lsoa_crime |> mutate(measure = "Per 1,000 residents", value = rate_res),
  lsoa_crime |> mutate(measure = "Per 1,000 workday population", value = rate_wkd)
) |>
  group_by(measure) |> mutate(quintile = factor(ntile(value, 5))) |> ungroup()
ggplot(three) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = quintile), colour = NA) +
  facet_wrap(~ measure) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "RdPu", name = "Quintile")
```

Which population is "at risk"? Residents, workers, visitors, dwellings, cars…?

## Same data, three classifications

```{r classes, fig.width=12, fig.height=4.8}
shade_by <- function(x, style) {
  as.integer(cut(x, unique(classIntervals(x, n = 5, style = style)$brks), include.lowest = TRUE))
}
classified <- bind_rows(
  lsoa_crime |> mutate(method = "Equal interval", class = shade_by(rate_res, "equal")),
  lsoa_crime |> mutate(method = "Quantile", class = shade_by(rate_res, "quantile")),
  lsoa_crime |> mutate(method = "Natural breaks (Jenks)", class = shade_by(rate_res, "jenks"))
)
ggplot(classified) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = class), colour = NA) +
  facet_wrap(~ method) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "RdPu", direction = 1, name = "Class\n(1 = lowest)")
```

Crimes per 1,000 residents. Calm or alarming? It depends on the break points.

## The modifiable areal unit problem

```{r maup, fig.width=12, fig.height=5.5}
manchester <- st_union(lsoa)
hex <- function(cellsize) {
  g <- st_make_grid(manchester, cellsize = cellsize, square = FALSE,
                    offset = st_bbox(manchester)[c("xmin", "ymin")] - cellsize) |>
    st_sf() |> st_filter(manchester)
  g$crimes <- lengths(st_intersects(g, crimes_bng))
  g$label <- paste0(cellsize, " m hexagons")
  g
}
hexes <- bind_rows(hex(200), hex(400), hex(800)) |>
  group_by(label) |> mutate(quintile = factor(ntile(crimes, 5))) |> ungroup() |>
  mutate(label = factor(label, levels = unique(label)))
ggplot(hexes) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = quintile), colour = NA) +
  facet_wrap(~ label) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "RdPu", name = "Quintile")
```

- **Scale effect:** results change with the size of the units.
- **Zoning effect:** results change with where the boundaries fall, even at the same size.
- Related: the **ecological fallacy** (area patterns ≠ individual behaviour).

➜ **Practical 2**

# Talk 3: Crime and place, and spatial operations {background-color="#5b2a86"}

## Why do some places have so much crime?

- **Crime generators:** places that attract lots of people for ordinary reasons, e.g. shopping streets, stations, stadiums. Crime follows the crowds.
- **Crime attractors:** places known for criminal opportunities, which draw motivated offenders.
- Brantingham & Brantingham (1995). Later work adds crime **radiators** and **absorbers**.

So are violent incidents concentrated around particular licensed premises?

## Spatial operations: joining by location

```{r buffers, fig.width=7, fig.height=5.5}
prem <- read.csv("../data/licensed_premises.csv") |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(27700) |> st_filter(city_centre)
viol <- crimes_bng |> filter(crime_type == "Violence and sexual offences") |> st_filter(city_centre)
buf <- st_buffer(prem, 50)
buf$violence <- lengths(st_intersects(buf, viol))
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = city_centre, fill = "grey95", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_sf(data = arrange(buf, violence), aes(fill = violence), colour = NA, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_sf(data = viol, size = 0.4, alpha = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Reds", direction = 1, name = "Violent crimes\nwithin 50 m")
```

**Select by location** (`st_filter`) · **buffer** (`st_buffer`) · **points in polygon** (`st_intersects`) · **nearest** (`st_nearest_feature`)

## Choices that change the answer

- **How near is "near"?** 25 m, 50 m, 400 m? Use theory or evidence, then test sensitivity.
- **Count or allocate?** Overlapping buffers count the same crime against several venues.
- **Compared with what?** Busy places have more of everything, so use a baseline such as random points or footfall.
- **Proximity is not causation.**

➜ **Practical 3**

# Talk 4: Spatial dependence {background-color="#5b2a86"}

## Spot the real map

```{r game, fig.width=10, fig.height=6.5}
burg <- lsoa |>
  left_join(crimes |> filter(crime_type == "Vehicle crime") |> count(lsoa21cd, name = "vehicle"),
            by = "lsoa21cd") |>
  mutate(vehicle = coalesce(vehicle, 0L))
set.seed(2024)
real_panel <- sample(1:4, 1)
game <- bind_rows(lapply(1:4, function(i) {
  vals <- if (i == real_panel) burg$vehicle else sample(burg$vehicle)
  burg |> mutate(panel = paste("Map", LETTERS[i]), value = vals)
}))
ggplot(game) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = value), colour = NA) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", trans = "sqrt", name = "Vehicle crime\nJune 2019")
```

One map is real. The others are the same values **shuffled at random**. Which is real?

::: {.notes}
The real map is in the panel given by `real_panel` (same seed as Practical 4). Ask for a show of hands, then reveal. Point out how hard it is, and that a permutation test is this game played 999 times.
:::

## Answer: Map `r LETTERS[real_panel]`

- Our eyes find patterns everywhere, so we need a **measure** and a **test**.
- Step 1: define **neighbours** (e.g. queen contiguity), the *spatial weights*.
- Step 2: the **spatial lag**, the average of the neighbours' values.
- Step 3: **Moran's I**, the correlation between a value and its spatial lag.
- Step 4: **permutation test**: compare with many random shuffles, as in the game.

## Moran's I for vehicle crime

```{r moran, fig.width=11, fig.height=4.8}
nb <- poly2nb(burg)
lw <- nb2listw(nb, style = "W")
burg <- burg |> mutate(z = as.numeric(scale(vehicle)), z_lag = lag.listw(lw, z))
set.seed(1)
mt <- moran.mc(burg$vehicle, lw, nsim = 999)
p1 <- ggplot(burg, aes(z, z_lag)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, colour = "#d7301f") +
  labs(x = "Vehicle crime (standardised)", y = "Spatial lag") + theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
p2 <- ggplot(data.frame(I = mt$res[1:999]), aes(I)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "grey70") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mt$statistic, colour = "#d7301f", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Moran's I under random shuffling (red: observed)", y = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
patchwork::wrap_plots(p1, p2)
```

Observed Moran's I = **`r round(mt$statistic, 2)`**, pseudo p = `r format.pval(mt$p.value, digits = 2)` (999 permutations).

## Where are the clusters? Local Moran's I

```{r lisa, fig.width=6, fig.height=5.5}
set.seed(1)
lisa <- localmoran_perm(burg$vehicle, lw, nsim = 499, alternative = "two.sided")
burg$p_adj <- p.adjust(lisa[, 5], "fdr")
burg$cluster <- ifelse(burg$p_adj < 0.05, as.character(attr(lisa, "quadr")$mean), "Not significant")
ggplot(burg) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = cluster), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("High-High" = "#d7191c", "Low-Low" = "#2c7bb6",
                               "High-Low" = "#fdae61", "Low-High" = "#abd9e9",
                               "Not significant" = "grey92"), name = NULL)
```

67 local tests means **adjusting for multiple comparisons** (here, FDR).

## Why it matters beyond maps

- Standard statistics assume **independent observations**. Neighbouring areas are not independent.
- Ignoring this means standard errors that are too small and false "significant" findings.
- Check model **residuals** for spatial autocorrelation, and use **spatial regression** (lag/error models) where needed.
- It's also substantive: diffusion, spillovers, shared context.

➜ **Practical 4**, then **Where next?**
